investment_summary:
Bloom Energy grew revenue 37.3% to $2,024.0 million in 2025, and gross margin rose to 29% from 27% [1]. The net loss widened to $88.4 million, or -$0.37 per share, after a $66.2 million convertible inducement charge, and operating cash flow was only $113.9 million [1][2].

Liquidity improved after the $2.5 billion 0% convertible notes, with cash of $2,454.1 million, but total debt nearly doubled to $2,992.0 million [1][2]. Consensus is dated after the 10-K: at about $153 the shares carry an enterprise value of about $45.5 billion, and consensus expects revenue growth of 123.6% in FY2026 and EPS rising to $5.35 by FY2027 [2][3].

The reverse DCF implies 48.8% annual revenue growth for ten years, against a 19.1% historical three-year CAGR, so the current price requires growth well above both history and the steep fade in consensus [2][3]. The implied return of 10.6% sits below the 15% WACC used [3]. Main risks are financing dependence, tax-credit policy and permitting for gas-fired systems [1]. Consensus rates the stock Buy with a mean target of $279.31 [3].
key_takeaways: Revenue momentum should carry into 2026 as Fremont scales to 2 GW; FY2026 consensus implies 123.6% growth, the key test [3].
Funding, not operations, is the binding constraint: $57.2 million of free cash flow cannot cover $2.99 billion of debt [1][2].
Valuation asks for more than history: the reverse DCF needs 48.8% annual growth for ten years, against 19.1% historically [2][3].
Gross margin expansion should continue as volumes scale: gross margin rose to 29% from 27% despite product-line charges [1].
business_overview:
Bloom Energy is a San Jose-based onsite power company that designs, manufactures, sells, distributes and operates the Bloom Energy Server, a high-temperature solid oxide fuel cell that converts natural gas, biogas or hydrogen into electricity without combustion or moving parts [1]. The same platform powers the Bloom Electrolyzer, which produces hydrogen, so the two products share a supply chain and manufacturing base [1]. Its core selling points are speed and reliability. Skid-mounted units can be installed in weeks or months and deliver power within about 90 days in certain project scopes, and the company reports fleet availability of about 99.9% for non-redundant installations and about 99.999% with redundancy [1]. The systems follow variable AI loads, which the company says respond at least twice as fast as turbines and engines, and they produce near-zero smog-forming pollutants [1]. Bloom holds 380 active U.S. utility patents and 183 pending applications [1].

The company serves three end markets: data centers, commercial and industrial customers, and utilities [1]. It has about 1,100 installed sites in nine countries. The U.S. is its largest market by revenue and installed base, and South Korea is second, with about 682 MW deployed [1]. Revenue is reported in four lines: product, installation, service and electricity. Product sales drove most of the 2025 growth, rising 41.1% to $1,531.3 million, while installation grew 66.8% to $204.1 million [1]. Sales cycles typically run 8 to 12 months, and installation takes six to twelve months or more after contract signing, which governs when revenue is recognized [1].

Management's agenda centres on capacity and financed growth. Fremont manufacturing is being expanded from 1 GW to a 2 GW annual run rate, targeted for completion by end-2026 [1]. An AEP supply agreement covers up to 1 GW, announced in November 2024 with an initial 100 MW order, and a prospective Brookfield financing framework covers up to $5.0 billion over five years [1]. Oracle has a partnership for on-site power at AI data centers, with a warrant for 3,531,073 shares [1]. The filing cites a 30% Section 48E investment tax credit for fuel cells that begin construction after December 31, 2025 [1]. At the consensus snapshot, the shares traded near $153 with a Buy rating and a mean target of $279.31 [2][3].
market_position:
Bloom sells into three end markets: data centers, commercial and industrial customers, and utilities [1]. The U.S. is its largest market by revenue and installed base, and South Korea is second, with about 682 MW deployed across roughly 1,100 sites in nine countries [1]. Demand is increasingly tied to AI data centers, which the filing describes as a significant increase in demand, and to a hyperscaler project routed through the Brookfield joint venture [1]. The filing does not disclose market share, so Bloom's standing can only be judged through its growth, margins and valuation relative to peers.

Customer concentration is high. Three customers or distributors accounted for 43%, 13% and 12% of 2025 revenue, and the 43% customer is a related party [1]. Together they make up 68% of revenue. That ties the revenue base to one hyperscaler's build schedule and weakens the independence of the largest account. Management's response is new capacity and partnerships: the AEP agreement for up to 1 GW, the Oracle on-site power partnership with a warrant for 3,531,073 shares, and the Brookfield financing framework of up to $5.0 billion [1]. Sales cycles of 8 to 12 months mean these agreements convert to revenue slowly [1].

Market sentiment has moved sharply. The 52-week range is $15.15 to $176.49, with a Buy consensus rating, a $279.31 mean target and a target range of $102 to $380 [2][3]. Market capitalization of about $43.5 billion [2] is far above the three peers in our set. Our view is that the valuation prices Bloom as an AI infrastructure supplier rather than a fuel-cell manufacturer, so the premium holds only while the order book converts into delivered revenue [3][4].
operating_results:
Revenue rose 37.3% to $2,024.0 million in 2025, from $1,474 million in 2024, led by product revenue, which grew 41.1% to $1,531.3 million [1]. Service grew only 6.9% to $228.3 million, and electricity rose 14.2% to $60.4 million [1]. Gross margin improved to 29% from 27%, but product gross margin declined year over year. Electrolyzer inventory reserves and impairments of $21.9 million, a $12.7 million construction-in-progress impairment, and a $15.9 million revenue reduction from share-based consideration to a hyperscaler customer all weighed on product margin [1]. Installation revenue rose 66.8% to $204.1 million, and its gross loss narrowed to $1.9 million [1].

Operating income improved to $72.8 million from $22.9 million, as gross profit rose $182.8 million while operating expenses rose $132.9 million to $514.6 million [1]. Service gross profit swung to $22.9 million from a $1.4 million loss, as lower field replacement unit deployment saved $29.4 million, although repair and overhaul costs rose $11.1 million as the fleet aged [1]. Electricity gross profit nearly doubled to $27.9 million, but that gain comes mainly from a one-time contract settlement and should not be treated as recurring [1].

Below operating income, other expense rose to $157.2 million from $49.3 million, including a $66.2 million debt conversion inducement and a $40.4 million equity loss from unconsolidated affiliates. The net loss widened to $88.4 million from $29.2 million, and diluted EPS was -$0.37 versus -$0.13 on 240.4 million average shares [1]. Operating cash flow was $113.9 million despite a $217.3 million working-capital outflow, and capex of $56.8 million left free cash flow of about $57.2 million, against $33.1 million in 2024 [1]. The operating profit was real, but below-the-line charges erased it at the net line. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, expects FY2026 EPS of $3.27 [3].
risk_assessment:
Demand depends on tax-equity financing and incentives. The filing says the fuel-cell investment tax credit was unavailable for natural-gas systems placed in service after December 31, 2024, except for safe-harbored property, and that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act restored a 30% credit through 2033 only for projects beginning construction after December 31, 2025 [1]. Incentives "may expire... or be reduced or terminated" and depend on continued political support [1]. The filing does not disclose what share of sales or backlog depends on these benefits, so the dollar exposure cannot be sized [1].

Demand timing is the second risk. Sales cycles of 8 to 12 months, and revenue recognized only on delivery or installation, mean small timing shifts can produce large quarterly misses [1]. The filing ties these cycles to interest rates, capital availability and recession, and warns that a slowdown in AI adoption or local siting restrictions could reduce demand [1]. The balance sheet amplifies the exposure: long-term debt was $2,613.7 million at year-end [1][2], and at the latest quarter total debt of $2,783.4 million and net debt of $296.7 million are dated after the 10-K [2]. Dilution adds to the risk, with the share count up 22.2% in 2025 and 25.0% year over year at the latest quarter [2].

Permitting for gas-fired systems is the third risk. Some municipalities have banned or are considering banning new gas interconnections, and some permits require costly renewable fuel blends [1]. Financial quality scores are mixed: the Piotroski F-score is 4 of 9, the Altman Z-score is 7.54, and the Beneish M-score of -2.59 gives no manipulation warning [2]. The three risks are linked, since a single delay in financing or permits could push several large projects back at once [1].
competitors_analysis:
We chose FuelCell Energy (FCEL) and Plug Power (PLUG) as the closest business models, because both build fuel-cell systems for stationary and hydrogen power, although both are much smaller and loss-making [4]. ERock (EROC) is third because it deploys distributed on-site power for commercial and industrial customers, close to Bloom's managed-services model, despite its short two-year history [4]. GE Vernova was excluded because it is about 11.5 times Bloom's revenue, a size mismatch [4].

Bloom leads on every metric the peers report in margin terms. Its 2025 gross margin of 29.0% compares with 20.7% at ERock and negative gross margins at FCEL and PLUG in all four years [4]. Its EBITDA margin was 1.0% in 2025, against -88.8% at FCEL, -223.1% at PLUG and -14.8% at ERock [4]. Revenue of $2,024 million dwarfs the peers, at $710 million for PLUG, $183 million for ERock and $158 million for FCEL, although Bloom's 37.3% growth trailed FCEL's 41.0% and ERock's 42.5% [4]. Bloom was the only company with positive free cash flow in two consecutive years, at 33 in 2024 and 57 in 2025, while FCEL and PLUG burned cash in every year shown [4].

The valuation gap is wide. Bloom's EV/Sales was 12.29 in 2025, against 1.76 at FCEL and 4.75 at PLUG, and its P/B of 31.66 compares with 0.29 to 1.70 at FCEL [4]. Its ROIC was -0.7% in 2025 after a single positive year in 2024, and EBITDA fell from $89 million to $20 million in the same year, even as gross profit rose to $587 million [4][2]. Consensus expects EPS to reach $3.27 in FY2026 and $5.35 in FY2027 [3], so the premium depends on that earnings path. The peer comparison supports Bloom's operating lead, but on its own it does not justify a premium of this size [3][4].

investment_theses.thesis: Bloom's revenue keeps compounding because AI and utility demand is converting into delivered sites.
investment_theses.evidence: Revenue rose 37.3% to $2,024.0 million in 2025 [1]; FY2026 consensus is $4,525.9 million, growth of 123.6% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: Fremont reaches a 2 GW annual run rate by end-2026, and FY2026 revenue lands within the $4.41-4.64 billion consensus range [3].
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 revenue falls below $4.41 billion, the low end of consensus, or Fremont completion slips past end-2026.

investment_theses.thesis: Bloom keeps relying on refinancing and equity issuance until operating cash flow covers its debt.
investment_theses.evidence: Free cash flow was $57.2 million in 2025 [1][2] against total debt of $2,992.0 million [1]; the share count rose 22.2% in 2025 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Share count growth below 5% year over year in the FY2026 10-K (early 2027), with full-year free cash flow positive.
investment_theses.invalidation: Share count grows more than 25% year over year again, or the convertible notes are settled in shares rather than refinanced.

investment_theses.thesis: The current valuation needs earnings to convert within two years; at today's price the market is paying for growth well beyond history.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 48.8% annual revenue growth for ten years versus 19.1% historically, and a 10.6% implied return against a 15.0% WACC [2][3].
investment_theses.signpost: A positive GAAP net income quarter in 2026, and FY2026 EPS consensus holding at or above $3.27 [3].
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 EPS consensus falls below $2.98, the bottom of its range [3], or the implied return stays under WACC after the next two reported quarters.

investment_theses.thesis: Gross margin expansion continues as volumes scale and one-off charges fade.
investment_theses.evidence: Gross margin rose to 29% from 27% [1]; product gross margin fell after $21.9 million of Electrolyzer reserves and a $12.7 million impairment [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Product gross margin is reported above its 2025 level in the Q1 2026 results, with no new Electrolyzer reserves.
investment_theses.invalidation: Consolidated gross margin falls back below 27%, the 2024 level, in any reported quarter.
